one_liner: Header-only LIFO container on chained, never-relocated memory blocks; author reports it beats std::stack over std::deque.
what_it_does: plf::stack<T, Allocator> offers the std::stack interface (push, emplace, pop, top, empty, size, swap) as a standalone container rather than an adaptor, plus extras std::stack lacks: reserve, shrink_to_fit, trim, append (splices another stack's blocks in), reshape of min/max block capacities, memory(), and bottom-to-top and reverse iterators. Pointers and references to elements stay valid until those elements are popped (shrink_to_fit() and reshape() relocate elements, so they invalidate them). It is close to a source-level drop-in for std::stack<T> with the default container, but its second template parameter is an allocator, not a container.
how_it_is_fast: Elements live in a doubly linked chain of memory blocks; when the top block fills, a new block sized to the current element count is allocated (so capacity roughly doubles) and nothing already stored is moved or copied, unlike a std::vector reallocation. pop() destroys the element (skipped for trivially destructible types), steps a cached top pointer back and keeps emptied blocks for reuse, so push/pop cycles across a block boundary do not hit the allocator; trim() releases them later. Compared with libstdc++'s std::deque, blocks are not capped at 512 bytes, which is why large element types (the README's 490-byte case) gain the most.
when_to_use: LIFO workloads (DFS, undo stacks, parsers, work lists) whose size swings widely, where std::stack's default std::deque spends time in allocation and block-map management.

Large or non-trivially-movable element types: the README's biggest gain (724% for 490-byte elements under libstdc++) comes where std::deque degenerates to one element per block and std::vector would have to relocate on growth.
Code that keeps pointers or references into the stack (inter-linked data) and needs them to stay valid while more elements are pushed.
Projects stuck on old compilers: the header still supports C++98/03 and adds move, emplace and allocator_traits support when the compiler has them.
when_not_to_use: Small trivially copyable elements (char, int) where a std::vector-backed stack with reserve() is competitive: per a search snippet of the author's own Haswell GCC 9.2 page, std::vector beat plf::stack for char, which contradicts the README's 'faster than all std:: containers' line (snippet only; page blocked here).

When you need the evidence reproduced: the README gives only averages and the benchmark code is not in any of the author's GitHub repositories; per search snippets the plflib pages used a Core2 E8500 with GCC 5.1 (-O2 -march=native) and a Xeon E3-1241 with mingw GCC 9.2, so the numbers say nothing about libc++ or MSVC STL deques.
Memory-sensitive code after a burst: popped-empty blocks stay allocated until you call trim(), shrink_to_fit() or clear().
Code using stateful allocators: get_allocator() returns a default-constructed allocator_type() instead of the stored one.
Generic code that relies on std::stack's adaptor surface (Container template parameter, the protected c member, construction from a container, operators <, <=, >, >=): only == and != are provided.

integration.dependencies: none outside the standard library; needs three files from the repo in one directory: plf_stack.h, plf_tools.h and plf_tools_undef.h (included at the end of plf_stack.h)
integration.min_toolchain: C++98/03 (features such as move, emplace and allocator_traits switch on by compiler version, e.g. MSVC 2010+ for move semantics); C++20 adds a std::reverse_iterator overload
integration.platforms: any (portable C++, no intrinsics on the stack path)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; no internal synchronisation, so treat it like a standard container (concurrent reads only).
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — push/emplace/pop/top/empty/size/swap match std::stack<T>, but the second template parameter is an allocator rather than an underlying container, there is no protected c member or container-taking constructor, only == and != comparisons exist, and emplace() returns void where C++17 std::stack::emplace returns a reference.

gotchas: Self copy-assignment (s = s, or a = *p with p == &a) asserts in debug builds; in release builds operator=(const stack&) calls destroy_all_data() before copying from the now-empty source, so the stack silently ends up empty.

get_allocator() returns allocator_type() rather than the allocator the stack holds, which is wrong for stateful allocators such as std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator and does not compile for allocators without a default constructor.
top() is declared const but returns a mutable reference, and top()/pop() on an empty stack are only checked by assert (undefined behaviour in release, as with std::stack).

The README's 'X% faster' figures are averages over 10 to 1,000,000 elements of construct, push all, read and pop all, destruct; the README does not say whether 82% means 1.82x throughput or 82% less time, and the 724% row reflects libstdc++'s 512-byte deque block limit rather than a general result.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over veque, fast_vector or eastl::vector when the workload is strictly LIFO, elements are large or must not move, or references into the container must survive growth; those siblings are contiguous vectors that suit small trivially copyable types and need a contiguous buffer. Use plf::list or plf::colony instead when you need erase from the middle or iteration-heavy unordered storage; plf::stack only adds and removes at the top.
verified_claims_summary: The README (first party) reports plf::stack 82%, 83%, 80%, 82% and 724% faster than std::stack over std::deque for 1-, 4-, 8-, 40- and 490-byte elements, averaged over 10 to 1,000,000 elements for construct, push, read-and-pop, destruct, against libstdc++; compiler, flags and CPU are not in the repo, and per search snippets the plflib.org benchmark pages (blocked here) used a Core2 E8500 with GCC 5.1 -O2 -march=native and a Xeon E3-1241 with mingw GCC 9.2, so it is not known which run produced the README averages.
status_note: Actively maintained (v2.0.37, 103 commits, last commit 2026-10-03, three issues all closed) under the Zlib licence; copyable as three headers, but the benchmark harness lives only on plflib.org, so the speed claim stays first-party.
